Data Privacy Basics

Scroll through each lesson to complete this course.

1. Why Data Privacy Matters

Every record your organisation holds about a customer or colleague is a promise: that the information will be used fairly, kept accurate, and protected from misuse. Privacy failures destroy trust faster than almost any other incident, and rebuilding that trust can take years. Regulators can also impose significant fines, but the reputational damage of a leaked database usually costs far more than any penalty. Treat personal data as something borrowed, never owned.

2. GDPR in Plain Language

The General Data Protection Regulation applies whenever you handle data about people in the EU. Its core ideas are simple: collect only what you genuinely need, use it only for the purpose you stated, keep it accurate, delete it when it is no longer required, and secure it at every step. Individuals can ask to see, correct, or erase their data, and your team must be able to respond within one month.

3. Strong Passwords and Passphrases

Length beats complexity. A passphrase of four unrelated words is far harder to crack than a short password full of symbols, and much easier to remember. Never reuse a password between systems: one breached website should never unlock your email. Use the company password manager to generate and store unique credentials, and switch on multi-factor authentication everywhere it is offered, especially for email and remote access.

4. Spotting Phishing Attacks

Phishing remains the most common way attackers steal data. Watch for urgency ("your account will be closed today"), unexpected attachments, and sender addresses that almost match a real one. Hover over links before clicking and check where they really lead. If a message asks for credentials, payment changes, or gift cards, verify by phone using a number you already trust. When in doubt, report it — a false alarm costs nothing.

5. Devices, Screens, and Clean Desks

Privacy is physical as well as digital. Lock your screen whenever you leave your desk, even at home. Keep laptops and phones encrypted and never leave them visible in a parked car. Collect printouts from the printer immediately and shred anything containing personal data when finished. In shared or public spaces, use a privacy screen and be aware of who can see your display or overhear your calls.

6. Reporting a Suspected Breach

Speed matters. If you lose a device, email the wrong recipient, or suspect an account is compromised, report it to the security team immediately — many regulations give organisations just 72 hours to notify authorities. Reporting early is never punished; hiding a mistake always makes it worse. Save the evidence, note the time, and let the response team take it from there. You have now completed this course.
